newsitem.title: SWEDEN: TENNIS-ENQVIST POISED TO SUCCEED EDBERG.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-ENQVIST POISED TO SUCCEED EDBERG.

text.p: Whether Sweden win or lose this weekend, the Davis Cup final against France represents a changing of the guard.
Stefan Edberg, the most elegant serve-and-volley exponent of his era, represents his country for the last time in his final major competition.

In Edberg's place a 22-year-old Stockholm native, currently ranked ninth in the world, is poised to take over as Swedish number one in a distinguished list including Bjorn Borg, Mats Wilander and Edberg.
Thomas Enqvist, playing in his maiden Davis Cup final, first picked up a racket at the age of five.
Coached by Joakim Nystrom, Enqvist won both the Australian Open and Wimbledon junior titles at the age of 17 thanks to a ferocious forehand.
In 1995 the 1.91 metre tall Swede, who now lives in Monte Carlo, started to make his mark on the international circuit.
He won five titles in six finals, including victories in Auckland, Philadelphia, Pinewhurst, Indianapolis, and Stockholm.
Enqvist also squeezed into the ATP Tour world campionship as a replacement where he advanced to the semifinals but was beaten by Boris Becker.
This year, after an indifferent start to the season, Enqvist has enjoyed a spectacular few months.

He clinched the Paris Open, beating Russian Yevgeny Kafelnikov in a game he described as "maybe my best match ever", and successfully defended his Stockholm Open title in a straight sets win over American Todd Martin.
At the ATP Tour world championship at Hanover last weekend, Enqvist also beat Boris Becker in a straight sets win after replacing Andre Agassi, who had withdrawn through illness.
Enqvist's five-set victory over Czech Daniel Vacek in September clinched Sweden's second Davis Cup final berth in three years.
"I have never faced a ball coming back at me like that," said a shell-shocked Korda. "If he can play like that on the tour, he can definitely be in the top five."
Sweden's assistant coach Anders Jarryd has no doubts about Enqvist's abilities.
"Edberg is the last of the old Swedish guard, Enqvist will be the cornerstone of the new guard," he said after the win in Prague.
Enqvist finds it difficult to believe he is now one of the world's top 10 players.
"It has not really sunken in yet that I am one of them," he said.
